question: Which statement about phenomena and things-in-themselves matches Week 3? Answer in 1-3 sentences.
model_answer: Objects may exist as things-in-themselves, but we know only their appearances. The lecture keeps existence and knowability separate: objects may exist in themselves, but cognition reaches only appearances.
key_points: Objects may exist as things-in-themselves, but we know only their appearances
The lecture keeps existence and knowability separate: objects may exist in themselves, but cognition reaches only appearances
it blocks the common confusion between epistemic limit and ontological denial
related_info: The lecture keeps existence and knowability separate: objects may exist in themselves, but cognition reaches only appearances.
why_high_yield: High yield because it blocks the common confusion between epistemic limit and ontological denial.
source_refs: HUMA2831_Week3_02162026_Slides.pdf - slide 7 on phenomena versus things-in-themselves

question: How does Week 3 distinguish sensibility from understanding? Answer in 1-3 sentences.
model_answer: Sensibility gives appearances, while understanding forms judgments about them. The lecture assigns raw appearing to sensibility and judgment to understanding.
key_points: Sensibility gives appearances, while understanding forms judgments about them
The lecture assigns raw appearing to sensibility and judgment to understanding
sensibility/understanding is one of the most repeated distinctions in the whole exam range
related_info: The lecture assigns raw appearing to sensibility and judgment to understanding.
why_high_yield: High yield because sensibility/understanding is one of the most repeated distinctions in the whole exam range.
source_refs: HUMA2831_Week3_02162026_Slides.pdf - slide 8 on sensibility versus understanding

question: What does Week 3 mean by saying understanding as a faculty is a priori and not in the phenomenal realm? Answer in 1-3 sentences.
model_answer: Understanding precedes and conditions experience rather than appearing as one empirical item within it. The lecture treats understanding not as one more thing seen in experience, but as a condition that makes objective experience possible.
key_points: Understanding precedes and conditions experience rather than appearing as one empirical item within it
The lecture treats understanding not as one more thing seen in experience, but as a condition that makes objective experience possible
it connects 'understanding' to the transcendental side of the course
related_info: The lecture treats understanding not as one more thing seen in experience, but as a condition that makes objective experience possible.
why_high_yield: High yield because it connects 'understanding' to the transcendental side of the course.
source_refs: HUMA2831_Week3_02162026_Slides.pdf - slide 10 on understanding as transcendental condition

question: How does Week 3 describe the human relation to reality? Answer in 1-3 sentences.
model_answer: Humans stand in relation to both the phenomenal and the metaphysical dimensions. The lecture says the human being stands in relation to two dimensions of reality, which is why metaphysics matters at all.
key_points: Humans stand in relation to both the phenomenal and the metaphysical dimensions
The lecture says the human being stands in relation to two dimensions of reality, which is why metaphysics matters at all
it frames why the course does not stop at mere empirical intelligence
